book.title: Odaklanma Gücü (The Power of Focus)
book.author: Jack Canfield (with Mark Victor Hansen and Les Hewitt)

confidence_note: The original English book is usually listed as co-authored by Canfield, Hansen and Hewitt and dated 2000, so the metadata was adjusted from the provided 1999. Canfield tells the $100,000-goal story often, most fully in The Success Principles (2005). It may appear only briefly in The Power of Focus or not at all. In Canfield's own telling he displayed a mock $100,000 bill, often said to be on the ceiling above his bed. He was not writing on a real $100 note stuck to a bathroom mirror. Placement details are therefore kept generic. The figures ($8,000 a year before, about $92,000 that year) are consistent across his accounts but should be presented as approximate. The car example for the reticular activating system is a common Canfield illustration, not a specific incident.
facts: Early in his career Canfield was earning roughly $8,000 a year.
He set a goal of earning $100,000 in one year, far beyond anything he had made before.
He made a mock $100,000 bill and put it where he would see it every day, so the goal stayed in front of him.
Over the following months, ideas and opportunities he had previously overlooked started to stand out to him.
That year he earned about $92,000. He fell short of the target but made more than ten times his previous income.
Canfield explains the effect through the reticular activating system (RAS), the brain's filter that decides which incoming information gets noticed.
His everyday illustration: once you consider buying a particular car, you suddenly see that model everywhere. The cars were always there, but your filter now flags them.
tension: A man earning $8,000 commits to a $100,000 goal. It seems absurd, and the question is whether simply looking at a number every day can change anything real.
opening_idea: Start with the gap: a modest yearly income beside a six-figure number taped up where he couldn't avoid it.

lessons.idea: A goal you see daily trains your attention to notice relevant opportunities that were already around you.
lessons.anchor: Reticular activating system / the car you suddenly see everywhere

lessons.idea: An ambitious target can pay off even when missed, because it stretches what you consider possible.
Making a goal concrete and visible turns it from a vague wish into something the mind treats as real.
lessons.anchor: The mock bill he looked at every day

reflect: Which of your goals exist only in your head, with nothing visible to remind you of them?
What opportunities might already be around you that your attention currently filters out?
Would you set a bigger target if missing it still left you far ahead of where you are now?
reflect_final: If your most important goal were written where you'd see it every morning, what would you start noticing that you miss today?

use_cases.situation: Setting a quarterly target with your team
use_cases.move: Write the single headline number on the team board or channel header and review it at the start of every meeting, instead of burying it in a slide deck.

use_cases.situation: Coaching someone who says their goal feels unrealistic
use_cases.move: Ask them to write the number down and put it somewhere they'll see daily for a month, then check in on what new options they've noticed.

use_cases.situation: Your own big goal keeps slipping out of mind
use_cases.move: Tonight, write the goal as one concrete number or phrase on a note and stick it where you look first each morning.

pocket_idea: Your brain notices what you tell it matters, so keep your goal where you'll see it.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: He missed a $100,000 goal and still made more than ten times his old income.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Canfield, earning about $8,000, looked at a mock $100,000 bill every day. His attention started catching opportunities, and he earned about $92,000 that year.
conversation_variants.question_idea: Ever decided on a car and then seen it everywhere? That's the same filter you can point at your goals.
conversation_variants.key_contrast_idea: A goal held vaguely in your head versus a goal you physically see every day.
